figure.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 340 152" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="65%" height="auto" style="max-width:442px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"><rect x="2" y="2" width="336" height="148" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#e2e8f0" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="22" y="28" font-family="system-ui" font-size="14" font-weight="800" fill="#0f172a">d</text><polygon points="170,20 132,48 146,92 170,92" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="1.4"/><polygon points="170,20 208,48 194,92 170,92" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#0f172a" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="170" y="128" text-anchor="middle" font-family="system-ui" font-size="13" font-weight="800" fill="#0f172a">1 half (1/2)</text></svg>

questions.hint: Look at the numerator (top number) and denominator (bottom number) of the fraction.

keyPoints.note: The denominator tells how many equal parts the whole shape is divided into, and the numerator tells how many parts to colour.

questions.solution: To show \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), colour \(1\) out of the \(2\) equal parts.

steps.explain: Check the denominator (bottom number) of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\): the shape is divided into \(2\) equal parts.

keyPoints.text: \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) of the pancake divided into \(4\) equal slices
keyPoints.note: Each of the 4 equal slices is 1 quarter of the pancake.

questions.solution: Since the pancake is divided into \(4\) equal quarters, shading \(\dfrac{3}{4}\) means shading \(3\) slices.

questions.stem: Look at the question in the speech bubble: "Is \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) more than \(\dfrac{9}{10}\)?" Which answer and reason are correct?

Yes, because fifths are larger pieces so \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) is larger than \(\dfrac{9}{10}\)
No, because \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) and \(\dfrac{9}{10}\) are exactly equal in size
Yes, because 5 is smaller than 10 so \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) is closer to 1 whole

steps.explain: Compare \(\dfrac{3}{5}\) and \(\dfrac{9}{10}\) on aligned fraction bars of the same whole. Each fifth equals \(2\) tenths (\(\dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{2}{10}\)).
